## Two bonds, one required return {.hook background-color="#FAF7F2"}

::: ask
1.  What is the **coupon yield** on a bond with face value $1,000, current
    price **$1,043.70** and a coupon rate of **8.25%**?
2.  What is the **price** of a three-year, **6%** coupon bond paying
    **semi-annually**, face value $1,000, if the required return is **8%**?
3.  One of these trades **above** par and the other **below**. Which, and why?
:::

::: notes
Same machinery as the problem we closed with last session, new numbers, and a
third part that is the whole point. Ten minutes.

Give them five minutes in pairs before anything is said out loud. Then take the
parts in order.

Part one is the easy one. The coupon is eight point two five percent of a
thousand, so eighty-two fifty a year. Divide by what you actually paid, which is
one thousand and forty-three seventy.

*[ask]* Before we divide - will the coupon yield be above or below eight point
two five percent?

Below, because the denominator is bigger than the face value. Seven point nine
zero percent.

Part two. Three years, six percent, paid semi-annually, market wants eight.

*[ask]* Three changes to the formula. What are they?

Halve the coupon - thirty, not sixty. Halve the rate - four percent per period.
Double the periods - six, not three. All three, every time.

Nine forty-seven fifty-eight.

*[pause]*

Now part three, and this is the one to spend time on.

*[ask]* The first bond costs more than a thousand. The second costs less. What
is different about them?

The first pays a coupon of eight point two five when the market is content with
less, so people bid the price up above face value until the return falls into
line. The second pays six when the market wants eight, so the price has to fall
below face value to make up the difference.

Write this down, because it is a one-line exam answer: **the price moves until
the yield matches what the market requires.** Premium means the coupon is
generous; discount means the coupon is mean. Nothing else is going on.

**Worked.** Coupon yield: 82.50 / 1043.70 = 7.90%. Price: six periods, coupon
30, 4% per period - 30 x [1 - 1.04^-6]/0.04 + 1000 / 1.04^6 = 157.26 + 790.31 =
947.58. First trades at a premium (coupon 8.25% > required), second at a
discount (coupon 6% < required 8%).
:::

# 3 · The stock market {.divider .center background-color="#06302F"}

## The residual claim {.hook background-color="#FAF7F2"}

A bondholder has a **contractual claim** to specified payments. A shareholder
owns a **residual claim**: whatever remains after the firm's obligations to
creditors and other senior claimants have been satisfied.

::: incremental
-   Equity returns come from **dividends** and **capital appreciation**.
-   Shareholders are **residual claimants** on the firm's assets and cash flows.
    They also typically hold **voting rights**, allowing them to influence major
    corporate decisions.
-   Because shareholders have **limited liability**, their payoff at liquidation
    cannot fall below zero, while their potential upside is unlimited.
-   This payoff structure can create conflicts between **shareholders and
    creditors**, particularly over **risk-taking**.
-   Separately, because shareholders delegate day-to-day decisions to managers,
    an **agency problem** arises: managers may pursue objectives that differ
    from those of shareholders.
:::

::: notes
Here is the difference between what we have been doing for two sessions and what
comes next.

A bondholder is owed a number. It is written in the contract. If the firm can
pay, they receive exactly that and not a cent more.

A shareholder owns what is left after everyone else has been paid. Which can be
a great deal, or can be nothing at all.

*[ask]* A company is about to be liquidated. Which claim would you rather hold?

*[ask]* Now a company about to triple in size. Which one now?

*[reveal the bullets one at a time]*

On the first two: returns come from dividends and from the price rising, and the
vote comes attached. Keep the vote in mind - it is the only one of these
instruments that carries any control over the firm.

*[pause on the third bullet, because it is the one that matters]*

Limited liability means the worst case is that your shares are worth zero. You
do not owe the firm's creditors anything beyond what you put in. So the downside
stops, and the upside does not.

Draw that asymmetry in the air with your hand, because they will meet it again
in an hour as the payoff diagram of a call option. It is the same shape.

*[fourth bullet]*

Now the consequence, and put it to them as a question.

*[ask]* You own shares in a firm that is close to default. The managers can take
a risky project: it either saves the firm or finishes it. Do you want them to
take it?

Yes - because you are nearly wiped out anyway, so you have very little left to
lose and everything to gain. And the creditors, who would have recovered
something in an orderly liquidation, want the opposite. That is the
shareholder-creditor conflict, and it is sharpest exactly when the firm is in
trouble.

*[fifth bullet]*

A separate problem, and do not let them merge the two. Shareholders own the
firm but do not run it. Managers do. Managers have their own objectives - size,
security, their own pay - and those do not automatically coincide with the
shareholders'. That is the agency problem, and you will meet it properly in
corporate finance.
:::

## 3 · The instruments: common, preferred, foreign

:::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Common stock** — the right to vote for directors and on certain issues, and
to receive dividends if the board declares them.

**Preferred stock** — usually **no vote**, but a **fixed dividend** paid before
common. Closer to a bond than most students expect.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Foreign stocks** — shares in a firm listed abroad. Useful for
diversification, but awkward to buy when they are not listed locally.

-   **American depository receipts (ADRs)** are the usual way to hold one: a
    bank buys the foreign shares and issues receipts against them that trade in
    dollars on a U.S. exchange.
:::
::::

::: notes
Common stock is what you picture: a vote, and a dividend if the board declares
one.

Preferred stock is the interesting one. Usually no vote. Fixed dividend. Paid
before common shareholders.

*[ask]* Fixed payment, paid ahead of others, no control. Is that equity, or is
that debt?

The honest answer is that it sits between the two, and that is exactly why
accountants and rating agencies treat it inconsistently. If you see it in a
balance sheet, look at how it has been classified — it is not always obvious.

On the right, the third category: foreign stocks. A share in a firm listed
somewhere else. Good for diversification, awkward to buy - different exchange,
different currency, sometimes different rules about who may hold it.

*[point at the sub-item]*

So an ADR is not a fourth kind of instrument. It is a way of holding a foreign
stock. If you want a Brazilian company but you can only trade in New York, a
bank buys the Brazilian shares, holds them, and issues receipts against them
that trade in dollars on a US exchange. What you own is still the Brazilian
company.

*[pause]*

If that sounds familiar, it should. It is the same engineering as the eurodollar
deposit from last session: take a claim, repackage it so it settles in the
currency and the legal system the buyer is comfortable with.

Close by saying where this goes next: we have the instruments, so the next
question is where they actually change hands.
:::

## 3 · Where the trading happens

:::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Organised exchanges**

-   NYSE trades roughly 4 to 7 billion shares a day.
-   "Organised" once meant a physical floor; electronic networks have largely
    replaced that idea.
-   **Listing requirements** exclude small firms.
-   Auction market with floor specialists; around 25% of trades filled directly
    by the specialist.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Over the counter**

-   NASDAQ is the obvious example, with roughly 3,000 securities listed.
-   **Dealers** stand ready to make a market — without one, the equity would be
    hard to trade at all.
-   Multiple market makers post bid and ask prices for the same security.
:::
::::

::: ask
Dealers quote a **bid-ask spread** and profit from it. Competition constrains
that spread — but a spread of zero would not be sustainable either. What costs
must the spread compensate the dealer for, and what happens to liquidity when
those costs rise?
:::

::: notes
Two ways to organise a market.

Exchanges on the left — one central place where orders meet. The New York Stock
Exchange still uses the word organised, but the trading floor you have seen in
films is mostly theatre now. It is computers.

Over the counter on the right. No central place. Dealers hold inventory and
quote you a price to buy and a price to sell.

*[ask]* The dealer buys from you at the bid and sells to someone else at the
ask, and keeps the difference. So why does competition not push that spread to
zero?

*[wait]*

Two reasons, and they are both real costs.

First, the dealer is holding inventory. They bought your shares and now they are
exposed until they sell them.

Second — and this is the one worth thinking about — some of the people trading
with the dealer know something the dealer does not. If you are selling to me
because you know bad news is coming, I lose. I cannot tell who those people are,
so I widen the spread against everyone.

*[ask]* Now, in a crisis, when nobody knows what anything is worth. What happens
to that second cost, and what happens to the spread?

It widens - and that is the whole point, because a wider spread *is* less
liquidity. The spread is what a round trip costs you, so when it doubles,
getting out has become twice as expensive. Then they cut the size they will
quote, and in the limit they stop quoting at all. That is what "the market
stopped" means: not that prices fell, but that there were no prices.

Now make the link explicit, because it is the same mechanism as the BNP Paribas
story we opened with last session.

Nobody could value the mortgage-related securities those funds held. So the
adverse-selection cost went through the roof - if you offer to sell me one,
perhaps you know your pool is the bad one. Dealers widened, then withdrew. With
no price, the funds could not value their own holdings, and a fund that cannot
compute what it is worth cannot let investors redeem. Hence the suspension.

And then it spreads, which is the part to leave them with: the same securities
were collateral for short-term borrowing. Collateral that cannot be priced is
collateral nobody will lend against, so funding dries up, which forces sales,
which pushes prices down further.

The sentence to land: liquidity is not a property of an asset. It is a service
somebody chooses to provide, and they stop providing it exactly when everybody
needs it.
:::

## 3 · Price-weighted versus value-weighted

An index is a **measuring instrument, not an asset**: one number tracking a set
of securities over time. The **DJIA** is price-weighted across 30 stocks; the
**S&P 500** is value-weighted across 500.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 4.6
dj <- fred("DJIA")
sp <- fred("SP500")
if (is.null(dj)) {
  no_data_note("DJIA")
} else {
  dj <- dj[dj$date >= as.Date("2015-01-01"), ]
  dj$index <- 100 * dj$value / dj$value[1]
  dj$series <- "Dow Jones Industrial Average"
  d <- dj[, c("date", "index", "series")]
  if (!is.null(sp)) {
    sp <- sp[sp$date >= as.Date("2015-01-01"), ]
    sp$index <- 100 * sp$value / sp$value[1]
    sp$series <- "S&P 500"
    d <- rbind(d, sp[, c("date", "index", "series")])
  }
  ggplot(d, aes(date, index, colour = series)) +
    geom_line(linewidth = .5) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = c(IF_COL$slate, IF_COL$teal500)) +
    labs(x = NULL, y = "Index, first observation = 100",
         title = "Thirty stocks by price, or five hundred by market value",
         caption = "Source: S&P Dow Jones Indices via FRED.") +
    theme_if()
}
```

::: ask
A USD 400 share moves the Dow **thirteen times** as much as a USD 30 one,
whatever the two firms are worth. So what is the Dow measuring?
:::

::: notes
Start with what an index is for, because they have heard the word for years
without ever being told.

An index is not something you buy. It is what you watch. When the news says the
market fell two percent, what fell was an index - one number built to monitor a
set of securities so you can follow it over time and compare it with other
markets.

*[ask]* If it is a measuring instrument, what is it measuring?

That is the whole slide. Two indices of the same market, two different answers
on the same day.

*[pause]*

Two indices, two completely different ideas.

The S&P 500 weights by market value. If a company is worth two percent of the
market, it is two percent of the index. That is what you would own if you bought
the whole market.

The Dow weights by *price per share*. Not by size. By the number printed on the
share.

*[ask]* So a four-hundred-dollar share and a thirty-dollar share. Which one
moves the Dow more?

The four-hundred-dollar one - about thirteen times more - regardless of whether
the companies are the same size or one is a hundred times bigger.

Now the step they usually miss, so take it slowly.

*[ask]* What decides whether a share costs four hundred dollars or thirty?

Not how big the company is. Price per share is market value divided by the
number of shares the firm chose to issue. Two firms worth exactly the same can
trade at four hundred and at four, purely because one issued ten times as many
shares. The price per share carries no information about size.

*[pause]*

Which is why the split is damaging. Two-for-one: each share becomes two, each
worth half. Same pie, twice as many slices. Same firm, same assets, same market
value - and its weight in the Dow has halved.

Then do the contrast, because it is what proves the point: under value weighting
the split changes nothing. Half the price, twice the shares, same market value,
same weight. A sound measuring instrument does not move when the thing it
measures has not moved.

If someone asks whether the index jumps on the split day: no, the divisor is
adjusted so the level is continuous. What that cannot fix is the weight.

*[ask]* So what is the Dow measuring?

Push them to a real answer rather than "nothing". It measures the return on a
portfolio holding one share of each of the thirty companies. That is a genuine
portfolio - it is simply not one anybody would hold on purpose, because there is
no economic reason to own equal *numbers* of shares across firms.

Contrast it with the S&P: when that moves two percent, the combined market value
of five hundred firms moved two percent. That is a quantity you can interpret.

*[ask]* So why does every news programme still quote the Dow?

Because it dates from 1896 and people recognise the number. That is a reason
from journalism, not from finance.
:::

Three formulas, three jobs: **value** the share from forecasts, **estimate** one
of the inputs, or value it **without forecasting at all**.

**1 · Value it.** The **Gordon growth model** — the dividend discount model with
dividends growing at a constant rate $g$ forever, and $k_e > g$:

$$P = \sum_{t=1}^{\infty}\frac{Div_t}{(1+k_e)^t} = \frac{Div_1}{k_e - g}$$

:::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
**2 · Estimate $g$.** Geometric growth, from two observations $n$ periods apart:

$$g = \left(\frac{\text{final}}{\text{initial}}\right)^{1/n} - 1$$
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**3 · Skip the forecast.** Price-to-earnings, a relative measure:

$$PE = \frac{\text{Price}}{\text{Earnings}}$$
:::
::::

::: keyidea
The denominator $k_e - g$ governs everything — and it is a **small difference
between two uncertain numbers**. As $g \to k_e$ the price explodes, so a
half-point revision moves the valuation enormously. Not a defect of the model,
but a property of perpetual growth.
:::

::: notes
Say the framing line first, because otherwise this looks like three unrelated
formulas dumped on one slide.

Three formulas, three jobs. The first values a share from your forecasts. The
second estimates one of the numbers the first one needs. The third values it
without forecasting anything at all.

Then take them in that order.

A share pays you dividends, forever. So its value is the present value of all of
them. Write that down and you get the sum on the left.

If the dividend grows at a constant rate g, that infinite sum collapses to the
expression on the right. Next year's dividend, over the required return minus
the growth rate. That is the Gordon growth model, and you have met growing
perpetuities before in corporate finance.

Two conditions, and they are not fine print. The growth rate has to be constant
forever. And k has to be bigger than g.

*[ask]* Why must k be bigger than g? What is wrong with a company that grows
faster than the required return, forever?

*[wait]*

Eventually it is bigger than the entire economy. That is your sanity check — if
you ever get g above k in the exam, you have made an arithmetic error, not
discovered a fantastic company.

Underneath: the PE ratio. Price over earnings. A market number on top, an
accounting number on the bottom.

*[ask]* A company has a PE of forty. Is it expensive, or is it expected to grow?

Both answers are right, and you cannot tell which from the ratio. That is the
limitation of every multiple.
:::

## 3 · The denominator does all the work

```{r}
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 4.2
div1 <- 2
p1 <- "Vary the required return k   (g stays at 5%)"
p2 <- "Vary the growth rate g   (k stays at 10%)"
lv <- c(p1, p2)

a <- data.frame(x = seq(.06, .20, length.out = 300))
a$price <- div1 / (a$x - .05); a$panel <- p1
b <- data.frame(x = seq(.00, .09, length.out = 300))
b$price <- div1 / (.10 - b$x); b$panel <- p2
d <- rbind(a, b); d$panel <- factor(d$panel, levels = lv)

base <- data.frame(x = c(.10, .05), price = c(40, 40),
                   panel = factor(lv, levels = lv))
asym <- data.frame(x = c(.05, .10), panel = factor(lv, levels = lv))

ggplot(d, aes(x, price)) +
  geom_vline(data = asym, aes(xintercept = x), colour = IF_COL$muted,
             linetype = "22", linewidth = .45) +
  geom_line(colour = IF_COL$clay, linewidth = .95) +
  geom_point(data = base, size = 2.6, colour = IF_COL$teal700) +
  geom_text(data = base, aes(label = "base case: 40"), nudge_y = 22,
            colour = IF_COL$teal700, size = 3.7, fontface = "bold") +
  facet_wrap(~panel, scales = "free_x") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = function(x) paste0(round(x * 100), "%")) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 200)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Price of the share",
       title = "Same share, same dividend of 2 next year - only the gap k - g changes",
       caption = "Dashed line: where k = g and the gap closes. Base case k = 10%, g = 5%, price 40.") +
  theme_if() +
  theme(strip.text = element_text(colour = IF_COL$teal700, face = "bold"))
```

::: notes
Before anything, tell them what is held fixed, or the picture means nothing.

Same company throughout. Same dividend of two next year. One base case: the
market wants ten percent, the dividend grows at five, so the price is forty.
That is the dot, and it is the same dot in both panels.

*[point at the left panel]*

Here I move only the required return and leave growth at five. Walk left from
the dot and the price climbs: ten to nine to eight percent, forty becomes fifty
becomes sixty-seven.

*[point at the right panel]*

Here I move only the growth rate and leave the required return at ten. Walk
right from the dot and exactly the same thing happens.

*[point at the dashed lines]*

Those mark where k equals g. In both panels the curve goes vertical there,
because the denominator has gone to zero.

*[pause]*

This is not a flaw in the model. It is what perpetual growth means. But look at
what it implies.

Near that edge, change your growth assumption by half a percentage point and the
valuation changes enormously.

*[ask]* So two analysts, same company, almost identical assumptions. How far
apart can their target prices be?

Very far. And that is why high-growth companies reprice so violently on news
that sounds small. Nothing happened to this year's earnings. Something happened
to the assumption in the denominator.

You have watched this happen — in 2000, and again in 2021 and 2022.
:::

## 3 · Problem 2.5

::: ask
1.  A stock is expected to pay a dividend of **$0.16** and to be worth **$60**
    in a year. At a **12%** discount rate, what is it worth now?
2.  If the industry PE ratio is **16** and the firm earns **$1.13 per share**,
    what is the price?
:::

::: notes
Two parts, one line each. But they are two different methods, and that is the
point.

Part one. You expect a dividend of sixteen cents and a price of sixty in a year,
and you discount at twelve percent. Sixty point one six over one point one two.
Fifty-three seventy-one.

Part two. The industry trades at sixteen times earnings, this firm earns a
dollar thirteen. Sixteen times one thirteen. Eighteen zero eight.

*[pause]*

Part one is a discounted cash flow. You forecast, then you discount.

Part two is relative valuation. You assume the market has priced similar
companies correctly, and you apply their multiple.

*[ask]* Which one do you trust more?

That argument is most of what equity analysts do for a living. Notice that the
first needs you to forecast, and the second needs the market to be right.

**Worked.** (0.16 + 60) / 1.12 = 53.71. And 16 x 1.13 = 18.08.
:::

## 3 · Problem 2.6

::: ask
The DJIA was **10,000** in 2010 and **20,000** in 2017. What was the annual
**geometric growth rate**?
:::

::: notes
Ten thousand in 2010, twenty thousand in 2017. What is the annual growth rate?

*[ask]* Careful. How many years is that?

Seven, not eight. Count the gaps, not the dates — that is the most common error
on this question.

So it is two to the power of one seventh, minus one. Ten point four one percent.

Notice the shape: the index doubled in seven years at about ten percent a year.
That is a useful number to carry around. Roughly seven years to double at ten
percent.

**Worked.** g = (20000/10000)^(1/7) - 1 = 2^(1/7) - 1 = 10.41%.
:::

# 4 · Mortgage markets {.divider .center background-color="#06302F"}

## The market that ate the world {.hook background-color="#FAF7F2"}

By 2006 an American mortgage was no longer a loan a bank made and held. It was
an input: pooled, tranched, rated, and sold on to a German Landesbank that had
never seen Ohio.

::: incremental
-   A mortgage is a **long-term loan secured by real estate**.
-   It is **amortised**: one fixed payment covers both interest and principal
    every month, so the balance falls to zero at maturity.
-   The security interest in the property is what makes the loan cheap. It is
    also what links the credit market to the housing market.
:::

::: notes
Set the scene before any definitions, because they already half know this story
and it will carry the section.

A mortgage is the most boring instrument in the chapter. A household borrows,
the house is the collateral, they pay a fixed amount every month for thirty
years. Nothing clever.

What made it interesting was what the banks did with it afterwards. By two
thousand and six, the bank that made the loan did not keep it. It sold it. It
got pooled with hundreds of others, sliced up, given a rating, and ended up on
the balance sheet of a regional bank in Germany that had never been to Ohio and
could not have found it on a map.

*[pause]*

Two definitions before we go on. Secured, which means if you stop paying, they
take the house - and that is why mortgage rates are lower than credit card
rates. And amortised, which means each payment does two jobs: it pays the
interest and it pays down some of the principal, so after thirty years you owe
nothing.

Hold on to the last line. The collateral is a house. So the credit market and
the housing market are not two markets. They are one.
:::

## 4 · The instruments: eight kinds of mortgage

| Type | What it is |
|:---|:---|
| Conventional | Not guaranteed; usually needs private mortgage insurance and 5-20% down |
| Insured | Guaranteed by a government agency; low or zero down payment |
| Fixed-rate | The rate is fixed for the life of the mortgage |
| Adjustable-rate (ARM) | Rate tied to another security, adjusted periodically within annual limits |
| Graduated-payment (GPM) | Low initial payment rising each year; amortises in 30 years |
| Growing-equity (GEM) | Payment rises each year; amortises in less than 30 years |
| Second mortgage | Secured by a second lien; used for credit lines and home improvement |
| Reverse annuity (RAM) | The lender pays the borrower monthly; due when the property is sold |

::: ask
Which of these transfer **interest rate risk** from the lender to the borrower,
and which households tend to be sold those contracts?
:::

::: notes
*[cuttable - if you are behind, show it for thirty seconds and move on]*

Do not read this table out. It is a reference slide, and they have it.

Point at two rows only.

Fixed-rate. The lender is locked in for thirty years. If rates rise, the lender
is stuck holding a loan that pays less than the market. The lender carries that
risk.

Adjustable-rate. The rate resets. If rates rise, the borrower's payment rises.
The borrower carries that risk.

*[ask]* So which of those two is cheaper on the day you sign, and why?

The adjustable one, because the lender has handed the risk to you and is giving
you a discount for taking it.

*[ask]* Now the uncomfortable half of the question. Who gets sold the
adjustable-rate contract with the low opening payment?

The households least able to absorb a payment that doubles. That is not an
accident of the product, it is how it was marketed, and it matters for what
happened in 2007.
:::

## 4 · Securitisation, in four steps

::: incremental
1.  The **secondary mortgage market** was created by the federal government
    after the Second World War, when it set up Fannie Mae. It grew quickly from
    the mid-1980s.
2.  Individual mortgages default unpredictably, so they are **pooled** —
    hundreds at a time — on the argument that diversification tames the risk.
3.  Rights to the pool's cash flows are sold as separate securities:
    **pass-throughs**, or mortgage-backed securities.
4.  The borrower's monthly payment passes through a trustee before reaching the
    investors.
:::

. . .

::: ask
Step 2 is load-bearing. Diversification removes risk that is **independent**
across loans. What becomes of a pool of American mortgages if house prices fall
**everywhere at once**?
:::

::: notes
This is the hinge of the whole session. Slow down here.

Four steps, and reveal them one at a time.

*[reveal 1]* The government built this market. Fannie Mae, after the war, to get
mortgages flowing.

*[reveal 2]* One mortgage is unpredictable - you cannot say whether this
household defaults. But put three hundred together and the law of large numbers
is supposed to do its work.

*[reveal 3]* Then you sell claims on the pool. The pool is the asset, the
securities are the claims.

*[reveal 4]* The household pays its monthly instalment, it goes through a
trustee, and it ends up with investors who have never met them.

*[pause, then put up the question and wait]*

*[wait - do not rescue them]*

Here is what they have to see. Diversification only removes risk that is
independent. If my neighbour defaulting tells you nothing about whether I
default, pooling works beautifully.

*[ask]* So - does my neighbour defaulting tell you nothing about me?

It tells you a great deal, if the reason is that house prices across the country
have fallen and we are both in negative equity. In that world the defaults
arrive together.

The correlation everyone had assumed was near zero turned out, in 2008, to be
near one. Every tranche above the very bottom had been priced on the assumption
it was near zero.

Say the general lesson plainly, because it is examinable: a diversification
argument is only as good as the independence assumption underneath it, and
nobody checks that assumption while it is working.
:::

## 4 · Mortgage rates track long Treasuries

```{r}
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 4.4
ids <- c(MORTGAGE30US = "30-year fixed mortgage", GS10 = "10-year Treasury")
series <- lapply(names(ids), function(id) {
  d <- fred(id)
  if (is.null(d)) return(NULL)
  d$series <- ids[[id]]
  d
})
series <- Filter(Negate(is.null), series)

if (!length(series)) {
  no_data_note("MORTGAGE30US / GS10")
} else {
  d <- do.call(rbind, series)
  ggplot(d, aes(date, value, colour = series)) +
    recession_bands(from = min(d$date)) +
    geom_line(linewidth = .5) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = c(IF_COL$slate, IF_COL$clay)) +
    labs(x = NULL, y = "Percent",
         title = "The mortgage rate is a spread over the long Treasury",
         caption = "Shaded: NBER recessions. Source: Freddie Mac and the Treasury via FRED.") +
    theme_if()
}
```

::: ask
The two series move together, but the **gap** between them is not constant.
What widens it?
:::

::: notes
Two lines, and the first thing to make them notice is that they move together.

*[ask]* Why would a thirty-year mortgage rate follow a ten-year government bond
rate at all? They are different instruments with different borrowers.

Because the lender has an alternative. If the government will pay me four
percent for lending to it, I am not lending to a household for less. The
Treasury yield is the floor, and the mortgage rate sits on top of it.

*[point at the gap]*

Now the gap. It is a spread, and a spread is a price for something.

*[ask]* Two things the household offers that the Treasury does not. What are
they?

Default risk - the household might not pay, the government will. And prepayment
risk - the household can refinance the day rates fall, so the lender loses the
good loans and keeps the bad ones.

*[point at a recession band]*

Look at what the gap does in the shaded periods. It widens, because in a
recession both of those risks get worse at the same moment.
:::

## 4 · Loan and annuity

:::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
What you can **borrow**, given what you can pay each period:

$$C_0 = a \times \left[\frac{1-(1+i)^{-T}}{i}\right]$$
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
What you must **pay** each period, given what you borrowed:

$$a = C_0 \times \left[\frac{i}{1-(1+i)^{-T}}\right]$$
:::
::::

```{r}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 3.6
n_m <- 20 * 12
rates <- c(.03, .05, .08)
labs_r <- paste0(round(rates * 100), "% a year")
pay <- seq(1000, 3000, by = 25)

d <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_along(rates), function(k) {
  i <- rates[k] / 12
  data.frame(a = pay,
             loan = pay * (1 - (1 + i)^(-n_m)) / i,
             rate = labs_r[k])
}))
d$rate <- factor(d$rate, levels = labs_r)

mark <- d[d$a == 2000, ]

ggplot(d, aes(a, loan, colour = rate)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 2000, colour = IF_COL$muted,
             linetype = "22", linewidth = .4) +
  geom_line(linewidth = .95) +
  geom_point(data = mark, size = 2.3) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(IF_COL$teal500, IF_COL$slate, IF_COL$clay)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = function(x) format(round(x), big.mark = " ", scientific = FALSE)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(1000, 1500, 2000, 2500, 3000)) +
  labs(x = "Monthly payment", y = "Loan you can support", colour = NULL,
       title = "Same 20-year term, same payment - three interest rates",
       caption = "At 2 000 a month: 361 000 at 3%, 303 000 at 5%, 239 000 at 8%.") +
  theme_if() +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

::: notes
One formula, written twice. Say that explicitly, because they will try to
memorise two things.

On the left: you tell me what you can pay every month, I tell you how much house
you can buy. On the right: you tell me the loan, I tell you the payment. Same
equation, rearranged.

Two warnings about i and T, and they are the same two as the semi-annual bond
from the warm-up. Monthly payments means a monthly rate - five percent a year is
nought point four one seven percent a month, not five. And T counts periods, not
years. Two hundred and forty, not twenty.

*[point at any one line]*

Each line is straight. Double the payment you can afford and you double the
loan. That part is dull.

*[point at the three dots on the dashed line]*

Now the same household, with two thousand a month to spend, at three different
interest rates. At three percent they can borrow three hundred and sixty-one
thousand. At five, three hundred and three. At eight, two hundred and
thirty-nine.

*[ask]* Their income has not changed by a cent. What has?

Only the rate. Going from three percent to eight takes a third of their buying
power away.

Say the consequence plainly, because it is the link to everything else in this
section:

Housing affordability is mostly a story about interest rates, not about prices
or incomes. And since this is what each household can bid, it is also what sets
house prices - which is why the mortgage-rate chart we just looked at is a
housing-market chart as much as a credit chart.

*[ask]* So when the central bank raises rates, what happens to house prices?

Hold that thought for the mortgage-market story - it is how 2006 begins.
:::

## 4 · Problem 2.7

::: ask
You want to borrow **$100,000**. Choose between a **12% 30-year** mortgage and
an **11.5%** mortgage with **2 discount points**. Which?
:::

::: {.smaller}
A discount point is 1% of the loan paid up front: on a $200,000 loan, 1 point
costs $2,000, half a point $1,000, a quarter point $500.
:::

::: notes
This is the one problem in the chapter with a genuinely conditional answer, and
that is why it is worth doing.

Set it up: two thousand dollars today, against fifty basis points saved every
month for thirty years.

*[ask]* Before any arithmetic - what is the one piece of information the
question has not given you?

How long you are going to stay in the house. Without that the question has no
answer, and spotting that is the skill being tested.

Then do the arithmetic. Both monthly payments from the annuity formula, take the
difference, and ask how many months of that saving it takes to earn back two
thousand dollars.

*[ask]* Suppose the break-even is around four years. You are a student who will
move cities for a job. Points, or no points?

No points. Same numbers, a family settling permanently: points.

The general lesson, and it recurs in the derivatives section: a cost paid up
front in exchange for a stream of savings is only worth it if you are around
long enough to collect the stream.

**Worked.** Two points on $100,000 is $2,000 today against 50 basis points saved
every month for thirty years. Compute both monthly payments with the annuity
formula, then ask how long it takes the saving to repay the $2,000. The answer
depends entirely on how long you stay in the house.
:::

# 5 · The foreign exchange market {.divider .center background-color="#06302F"}

## The biggest market nobody sees {.hook background-color="#FAF7F2"}

No building, no opening bell, no ticker on the evening news. Over the counter,
bank to bank, with turnover in the **trillions of dollars a day**.

::: incremental
-   What is traded is not currency in the sense of notes, but **bank deposits
    denominated in different currencies**.
-   Trades are large — typically in excess of USD 1 million.
-   We met the **price** in session 2. Now we meet the **market** that sets it.
:::

::: notes
A short section, and the job is to connect it to what they already did.

*[ask]* Name the largest financial market in the world.

They will say New York, or the stock market. It is this one, and most of them
have never seen a picture of it, because there is nothing to photograph. No
floor, no bell, no building.

*[pause]*

The second line matters more than it looks. What changes hands is not banknotes.
It is bank deposits. When a French importer buys dollars, nobody counts out
dollars - one bank's dollar deposit is credited, another's is debited.

Why insist on that? Because it is the reason this market is enormous and
invisible at the same time, and the reason it is bank to bank rather than on an
exchange.

Last line, and say it directly: in session two we spent a long time on the
exchange rate as a price. We did supply and demand for baht, we did the fixed
versus floating table. Today is the other half - the market where that price is
actually made.
:::

## 5 · Purchasing power parity

Both versions rest on the **law of one price**: if the same good is cheaper in
one country, arbitrage moves goods until the two prices converge.

:::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Absolute PPP** — about **levels**. The exchange rate equals the ratio of the
two price levels:

$$E_{\$/\mathrm{EUR}} = \frac{P_{US}}{P_{EUR}}$$

Needs identical baskets and no trade frictions, so it rarely holds exactly.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Relative PPP** — about **changes**. Depreciation equals the inflation
differential:

$$\frac{\Delta E_{\$/\mathrm{EUR}}}{E_{\$/\mathrm{EUR}}} = \pi_{US} - \pi_{EUR}$$

Constant frictions cancel out, so this is the version that can be tested.
:::
::::

It **fails in the short run** on two counts: goods are differentiated, so firms
hold pricing power and identical goods do not carry identical prices; and prices
are **sticky**, so they do not adjust quickly. Both break the arbitrage. It
**holds in the long run** because sticky prices eventually unstick — PPP
describes the destination, not the journey.

::: notes
Start with the intuition, not the formula, because the formula is only the
intuition written down.

The idea is the law of one price. If the identical good costs more in one
country than another, someone buys it where it is cheap, sells it where it is
dear, and the trade pushes the prices together.

*[left column]*

Do that for every good at once and you get absolute PPP. The exchange rate is
the ratio of the two price levels. Say plainly that it almost never holds
exactly - identical baskets and frictionless trade are a lot to ask.

*[right column]*

Relative PPP is the same statement in rates of change, and the difference is
what makes it usable. If American inflation runs two points above European
inflation, the dollar should lose about two percent a year against the euro.

The reason this version survives: a constant friction - transport, a tariff, a
retail margin - shifts the level but not the rate of change, so it cancels. That
is why absolute PPP fails on the data and relative PPP is the one that gets
tested.

*[the paragraph below]*

Two reasons it fails in the short run, and both are failures of the arbitrage.

Goods are not identical. Brands, trademarks and legal protection give firms the
power to charge different prices in different countries and keep doing it.

And prices are sticky. Even where arbitrage would work, prices do not adjust
quickly, so the gap persists for years.

Then the long run, in one line: sticky prices eventually unstick. PPP is a
statement about where things end up, not about next quarter - which is exactly
why it is useless for forecasting and still worth knowing.
:::

## 5 · The instruments: spot and forward

:::: columns
::: {.column width="46%"}
**Spot rate** — near-immediate exchange of bank deposits.

**Forward rate** — exchange at an agreed future date, at a price agreed now.
:::

::: {.column width="54%"}
Rates move when the demand for or supply of a currency moves, which happens on
expected changes in:

-   **relative price levels**
-   **trade barriers** — tariffs and quotas
-   **preferences** for domestic versus foreign goods
-   **relative productivity**
:::
::::

. . .

::: keyidea
Every item on that list is an **expected** change. Today's spot rate is mostly a
statement about tomorrow.
:::

::: notes
Two rates, and the difference is only timing. Spot: we exchange now. Forward: we
agree the price now and exchange in three months.

*[ask]* Who needs the forward one? Give me a firm and a reason.

A French exporter who has invoiced an American customer in dollars and will be
paid in ninety days. They know the amount in dollars. They do not know what it
will be worth in euros. The forward removes that uncertainty - and note that it
removes it in both directions, which is the same structure as the hedge we meet
in the derivatives section.

*[point at the list on the right]*

Four things that move the rate. Do not drill the list.

*[reveal the key idea]*

Drill this instead. Every item on that list is an expected change, not a current
one.

*[ask]* Inflation data comes out this morning, exactly as everyone predicted.
What happens to the exchange rate?

Nothing. It was already in the price. The rate moves on surprises, and that is
why exchange rates are so hard to forecast: you would be forecasting the part
nobody expected.
:::

## 5 · What an appreciation does

::: incremental
-   Domestic goods become **more expensive abroad**; foreign goods become
    **cheaper at home**.
-   Domestic producers become **less competitive** in both markets.
-   Domestic consumers gain **purchasing power**.
:::

. . .

::: ask
So is a strong currency good news? Ask a French exporter and a French
holidaymaker on the same afternoon and you will get two answers.
:::

::: notes
*[cuttable - the content is in the previous two slides if you are short]*

Short slide, and the point is distributional.

*[reveal the three bullets one at a time]*

The euro appreciates. French wine costs more in New York. American machinery
costs less in Lyon. So French producers lose on both sides, and French consumers
win.

*[pause]*

*[ask]* The euro strengthens ten percent. Good news or bad news?

Push back on whichever answer you get, because the question is badly posed on
purpose.

It is good news if you are flying to New York next week. It is bad news if your
job is making the wine. A currency movement is not good or bad for a country -
it is good for some people in it and bad for others, and the people it is bad
for are usually better organised politically.

*[ask]* So which group do governments tend to listen to?

That is why "currency manipulation" is a political accusation and not just an
economic one.
:::

# 6 · Derivative markets {.divider .center background-color="#06302F"}

## A price for a promise {.hook background-color="#FAF7F2"}

In 1995 Barings Bank, 233 years old, was destroyed in a matter of weeks by one
trader's position in Nikkei futures. The instruments were not exotic. The
position was simply unhedged and unsupervised.

::: incremental
-   A **derivative** is a contract whose value comes from the price of something
    else — an index, a rate, a currency, a tonne of wheat. You never own the
    thing itself; you own a claim written on its price.
-   They exist because **risk can be sold**: one party wants rid of it, another
    will carry it for a price.
-   **Hedging** is taking a second position that moves against a risk you
    already carry, so the two cancel.
-   Taken on its own, that same contract is a **bet**. A hedge and a speculation
    are the same instrument — the difference is whether you already hold what it
    is written on.
:::

::: notes
Open with Barings, because it does the work of three slides of warnings.

A bank that had been trading since seventeen sixty-two. It financed the
Louisiana Purchase. One trader in Singapore, positions in Japanese index
futures, and in a matter of weeks there was no bank. It was sold for one pound.

*[ask]* What do you think the instruments were - something exotic that nobody
understood?

No. Index futures. The most standardised, most transparent, most boring
derivative there is. Nothing about the instrument was the problem.

*[pause, then reveal the bullets one at a time]*

First: derivative means derived. The contract is worth something only because
something else has a price - an index, a rate, a currency, a tonne of wheat. You
never own the wheat. You own a piece of paper whose value tracks the wheat.

*[ask]* Why would anyone write such a contract? What is being traded?

Second line, and this is the one that explains why the market exists. What is
being traded is risk. A farmer wants rid of the risk that the March price
collapses. Somebody else will carry that risk, for a price. The contract is the
transfer, and the price of the contract is the price of the risk.

Third: hedging. You already carry a risk, so you take a second position that
moves the other way, and the two cancel. Note the words *already carry* - they
are doing all the work in that sentence.

*[pause]*

Fourth line, and this is Barings in one sentence. Strip away the risk you
already carry, and what is left is the contract on its own - which is a bet.

*[ask]* So what was Leeson doing - hedging or speculating?

Speculating, and the instrument cannot tell you which. The same futures contract
is prudent in the hands of someone holding Japanese shares and ruinous in the
hands of someone who is not. Nothing in the contract distinguishes them, which
is exactly why supervision rather than the instrument is the subject of that
story.
:::

## 6 · Long, short, and offsetting

:::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
A **long** position: you own the asset and gain if the price rises.

A **short** position: you do not own it — you borrow it, sell it, and gain if
you can buy it back cheaper.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
To **hedge**:

-   a long position is offset by taking an additional **short** position
-   a short position is offset by taking an additional **long** position
:::
::::

::: keyidea
Hedging is not the absence of a position. It is **two** positions, chosen so
that what one loses, the other gains.
:::

::: notes
*[cuttable - but only if they already have long and short from another course]*

*[ask]* Long and short. Who can define them?

Long is easy: you own it, you want it to go up.

Short is the one worth pausing on. You borrow the share from someone, sell it
today, and you owe them a share back. So you are hoping to buy it back cheaper.

*[ask]* What is the worst that can happen to someone who is long?

The price goes to zero. They lose what they put in.

*[ask]* And the worst that can happen to someone who is short?

There is no worst. The price has no ceiling, so the loss has no ceiling. Write
that asymmetry down - it is the same asymmetry as the one between the option
buyer and the option writer later in this section.

*[point at the key idea]*

Last line, and it is the definition they should leave with. A hedge is not
having no position. It is having two, pointing opposite ways, so the gain on one
pays for the loss on the other.
:::

## 6 · The instruments: five families

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Forwards

-   An agreement between two parties to transact at a **future point in time**.
-   Specifies the exact assets, the price, and the date of exchange.
-   **Long** = agree to buy later. **Short** = agree to sell later.
-   Private and bilateral, and therefore exposed to the other party defaulting.

### Futures

-   The same idea, traded on an **organised exchange** rather than privately.
-   **Standardised**, and therefore far more liquid than forwards.
-   **Marked to market daily**, which is what removes most of the default risk.
-   No need to deliver: positions are netted in cash.
-   Harder to corner, because the deliverable range of securities is wide.
-   Regulated in the United States by the CFTC.

### Options

-   The **right, not the obligation**, to buy (**call**) or sell (**put**) at
    the strike price.
-   **American** options may be exercised up to expiry; **European** options
    only on the expiry date.
-   You pay a **premium** for that right. The premium rises with **time to
    expiry** and with **volatility**, and moves with the strike.

### Swaps

-   An **interest-rate swap** exchanges one stream of interest payments for
    another, in the same currency.
-   The **plain vanilla** version specifies the rates exchanged, the type of
    payments, and the notional amount.
-   No balance-sheet change, and longer-dated than futures or options — but
    **illiquid** and exposed to **default risk**.

### Credit

-   **Credit derivatives** pay off on changes in credit events. The notional
    outstanding is in the trillions.
-   **Credit options** are tied to ratings or spreads.
-   **Credit swaps** exchange payments on loan portfolios, letting lenders
    specialise locally while diversifying.
-   A **credit default swap** pays off, option-like, when a basket of loans
    defaults.

:::

::: notes
Five tabs. Do not read them. Take forwards and futures together, spend real time
on options, name swaps, and finish on credit.

*[forwards and futures tabs]*

Forwards and futures are the same promise. I agree today to buy from you in
March at a price we fix now. The difference is only where it is done.

*[ask]* A forward is a private agreement between us. What is the risk that
creates?

That in March, when the price has moved against you, you do not turn up. The
exchange solves that - futures are standardised and marked to market every
single day, so nobody is ever owed more than one day's movement.

*[options tab]*

Now the one that is genuinely different. A future obliges you. An option gives
you the right and lets you walk away.

*[ask]* If I am handing you the right to walk away, what do I want in return?

A premium. And the premium goes up with time to expiry and with volatility -
both of which are just saying the same thing, that more can happen between now
and then.

*[swaps tab]* Name it and move on. Two streams of interest payments exchanged.
Enormous market, no balance-sheet change, illiquid, default risk.

*[credit tab]*

Finish here deliberately. A credit default swap pays you when a basket of loans
defaults. It is insurance on someone else's borrowing.

*[ask]* And can you buy that insurance on a house that is not yours?

Yes. You can, and in 2007 people did, in volumes far larger than the loans
themselves. Hold that thought for the regulation session.
:::

## 6 · Why the payoff diagram is the whole lesson

```{r}
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 4.2
S <- seq(105, 130, length.out = 300)
K <- 115; prem <- 2000; mult <- 400
call <- data.frame(S = S, profit = pmax(S - K, 0) * mult - prem,
                   who = "Buyer of call option", panel = "Call option and long future")
futl <- data.frame(S = S, profit = (S - K) * mult,
                   who = "Buyer of futures", panel = "Call option and long future")
put  <- data.frame(S = S, profit = pmax(K - S, 0) * mult - prem,
                   who = "Buyer of put option", panel = "Put option and short future")
futs <- data.frame(S = S, profit = (K - S) * mult,
                   who = "Seller of futures", panel = "Put option and short future")
d <- rbind(call, futl, put, futs)

ggplot(d, aes(S, profit, colour = who)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = IF_COL$muted, linewidth = .3) +
  geom_line(linewidth = .8) +
  facet_wrap(~panel) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = unname(unlist(
    IF_COL[c("clay", "slate", "clay", "slate")]))) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = function(x) format(x, big.mark = " ", scientific = FALSE)) +
  labs(x = "Price at expiration", y = "Profit",
       title = "The option has a floor. The future does not.",
       caption = "Strike 115, premium 2 000 per contract.") +
  theme_if() +
  theme(strip.text = element_text(colour = IF_COL$teal700, face = "bold"))
```

-   The **strike** is the price written into the option — the price at which you
    may buy (call) or sell (put). It is fixed for the life of the contract while
    the market price moves. Here it is **115**.
-   The **future** is a straight line through it: gain above, loss below, and
    nothing underneath to stop the fall.
-   The **option** follows that line above the strike, then goes **flat** — below
    it you simply do not exercise, so the loss stops at the premium.
-   On the right it sits **below** the future by exactly that premium. That is
    what the floor cost you.
-   So you **buy the bend by giving up part of the upside**, which is worth
    paying for when you could not survive the straight line continuing down.

::: notes
Do not cut this slide. If they understand one picture from the derivatives
section, it is this one.

*[name the strike before anything else]*

The strike is the number written into the contract - the price at which the
holder may buy or sell. It never changes; the market price does. So it is the
line in the sand that decides whether exercising is worth anything, and it is
exactly where the picture bends. On this chart it is 115.

*[ask]* The market ends at 120, strike 115. Do you exercise?

Yes - you buy at 115 something worth 120. And at 110? No, you walk away and buy
in the market. That switch is the bend.

*[point at the straight line first]*

The future is a straight line through the strike. Price goes up, you gain. Price
goes down, you lose, and there is nothing underneath you.

*[now trace the option line with a finger, from the right-hand side leftwards]*

The option is the same line on the right - and then it stops falling. It goes
flat. Below the strike you simply do not exercise, so your loss stops at the
premium you paid.

*[ask]* So where is the option line *below* the futures line?

On the right, everywhere. The option buyer always ends up two thousand worse off
than the futures buyer when the price rises, because that is what the premium
cost.

*[pause]*

Say the trade-off as one sentence and ask them to write it: you buy the bend by
giving up part of the upside.

*[ask]* When is that worth doing?

When the downside would actually hurt you - when you could not survive the
straight line continuing downwards. That is the answer to both of the problems
that follow.
:::

## 6 · Problem 2.8

Rock Solid holds a **$100 million** stock portfolio that tracks the S&P 500.
The manager fears a decline and wants to hedge the downside completely.

::: ask
1.  The S&P is at **1,000**. How is the hedge constructed with **futures**?
2.  What happens if a year later the index is at **900**?
3.  And if it is at **1,100**?
:::

::: {.smaller}
An index futures contract has a multiplier of **250**, so one contract is worth
$250 \times 1000 = \$250{,}000$.
:::

::: notes
Five minutes in pairs, then take it apart on the board.

*[ask]* The portfolio is long the index. Which way does the hedge point?

Short. Sell futures.

*[ask]* How many contracts?

One hundred million divided by two hundred and fifty thousand. Four hundred
contracts, sold short.

Now the two states of the world, and do them both.

At nine hundred: the index has fallen ten percent, so the portfolio loses ten
million. The short futures position gains ten million. Net zero.

At eleven hundred: the portfolio gains ten million, and the futures lose ten
million. Net zero.

*[pause]*

This is where the misunderstanding lives, so put the question to them directly.

*[ask]* Is that what the manager wanted?

They wanted protection on the way down. What they bought was no exposure at all,
in either direction. A futures hedge is symmetric - it does not know which way
you were hoping the market would go.

**Worked.** 400 contracts sold short. At 900 the portfolio loses 10m and the
futures gain 10m. At 1100 the portfolio gains 10m and the futures lose 10m. The
hedge works in both directions, which is the point students miss.
:::

## 6 · Problem 2.9

The same portfolio and the same fear. Now the S&P is at **1,000**, and a strike
of **950** costs a premium of **$200 per contract**.

::: ask
1.  How is the hedge constructed with **options**?
2.  What happens at **900**?
3.  What happens at **1,100**?
:::

::: {.smaller}
An index option contract has a multiplier of **100**, so one contract is worth
$100 \times 1000 = \$100{,}000$.
:::

::: notes
Same portfolio, same fear, different instrument - so the only honest way to do
this one is side by side with 2.8.

*[ask]* Long the index, and you want protection on the way down. Call or put?

Puts. You buy the right to sell.

Contracts: one hundred million over one hundred thousand. One thousand
contracts, and the premium is two hundred each, so two hundred thousand dollars
leaves the fund today whatever happens next.

At nine hundred: the puts are in the money below nine fifty, so they pay. But
notice the portfolio fell from a thousand to nine hundred and the protection
only starts at nine fifty - the first fifty points are uncovered. That gap is a
deductible, and it is there because they chose that strike.

At eleven hundred: the puts expire worthless, you have lost the premium, and you
keep the whole ten million gain.

*[pause]*

*[ask]* So compare the two problems in one sentence each.

The future gave away the upside and cost nothing up front. The option kept the
upside and cost two hundred thousand up front, with a gap at the bottom.

*[ask]* Which is the better hedge?

Neither. They are different products at different prices, and the right answer
depends on whether the fund can live with the gap and whether it needs the
upside. That is the bend from the payoff diagram, with numbers on it.

**Worked.** 1,000 put contracts at strike 950, premium 200 each = $200,000 paid
today. At 900 the puts pay but the first 50 index points are uncovered. At 1,100
the puts expire worthless and the portfolio keeps the full gain.
:::

# 7 · Reading discussion {.divider .center background-color="#06302F"}

## Does a green label change the price? {.hook background-color="#FAF7F2"}

A green bond funds an environmental project. In every other respect it is an
ordinary bond from an ordinary issuer, with the same claim on the same balance
sheet.

::: incremental
-   If the cash flows and the credit risk are identical, should it trade at a
    different yield?
-   If it should not, what exactly is the instrument **for**?
:::

::: notes
This is the reading discussion, and it is assessed, so protect the time for it.
Do not let the derivatives section eat it.

Open with the puzzle rather than the paper.

A green bond is a bond. Same issuer, same balance sheet, same legal claim, same
seniority in default. The only difference is a promise about what the money is
spent on.

*[reveal the first bullet, then ask]*

*[ask]* Identical cash flows, identical credit risk. Should it yield less than
the ordinary bond?

Let them argue. The finance answer is no - price the cash flows, and these cash
flows are the same. Any yield difference is investors paying for something other
than return.

*[reveal the second bullet]*

*[ask]* Then what is the instrument for?

Three candidates worth having on the board before you open the paper:
a signalling device, a marketing device, or a commitment device. The paper is
largely an argument about which of the three it actually is.
:::

## 7 · Sartzetakis (2021), green bonds and the low-carbon transition

::: {.panel-tabset}

### The questions

Come with an answer to each of these. I will ask.

1.  What are the **advantages and disadvantages of enlarging the mandate of the
    central bank**?
2.  Which projects can be considered **"green"** and financed by green bonds?
3.  What is the process for **project evaluation and selection**?
4.  What are the **positive developments** in the green bond market, and the
    **limits** to its development?

### How to prepare

-   Question 1 is the contested one. A central bank with a climate mandate is
    making distributional choices it was not elected to make — against the
    argument that climate risk is financial risk and therefore already within
    its remit.
-   Questions 2 and 3 are where **greenwashing** lives. If the issuer defines
    "green" and the issuer appoints the verifier, what is the label worth?
-   For question 4, separate market **growth** from market **effect**. A market
    can grow quickly and still finance nothing that would not have been financed
    anyway.

:::

::: notes
Run this as a discussion, not a lecture. If you are talking for more than two
minutes at a stretch, stop.

Structure: ten minutes in pairs on questions two and three, then open the floor
on question one, then close on four.

On question one, make sure both sides get stated. For: climate risk is financial
risk, so it is already the central bank's job. Against: deciding which sectors
get cheap funding is fiscal policy, and nobody voted for the central bank.

*[ask, if the room is quiet]* Who should decide which industries get cheap
credit - a parliament, or a committee of unelected economists?

On two and three, push them to the mechanism rather than the opinion. Who writes
the definition of green? Who checks it? Who pays the person who checks it?

On four, hold them to the distinction between growth and effect, and then close
the loop with the start of the session:

If the green label does not move the yield, the issuer gets no cheaper funding
from it. And if they get no cheaper funding, the only reason to issue one is
reputation. That is the paper's problem in one sentence, and it is the sentence
I want back in the exam.
:::
